newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli, PLO security officials meet after bombing.
newsitem.headline: Israeli, PLO security officials meet after bombing.

text.p: Israeli and Palestinian security officials met late into the night amid bitter recriminations over a suicide bombing in which a Palestinian Moslem killed three women in a Tel Aviv cafe.

"The peace process is in jeopardy at this point. If the Palestinians do not do what we are asking them to do by way of fighting terrorism it is very doubtful that the process can continue," David Bar-Illan, Prime Minister's Benjamin Netanyahu's communications director, told Reuters.
The Friday blast, which wounded 42 people, was a blow to faltering Middle East peace-making.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat condemned it, and telephoned Netanyahu to express condolences but the prime minister accused Arafat's Palestinian Authority of indirectly giving the green light to attackers.

The Palestinian security chief in Gaza, Mohammad Dahlan, told Reuters "Netanyahu's accusation against President Arafat are simply an attempt to divert attention from the responsibility he himself bears for these attack."
Ami Ayalon, Israel's Shin Bet secret police head, held talks at an undisclosed location in Tel Aviv with Dahlan and another Palestinian security chief, Mohammad Jibril Rajoub, security sources said.
"We are telling them (the Palestinians) they must co-operate in combating terrorism," Bar-Illan said.
Bar-Illan said Israel was demanding, among other things, that the Palestinians crackdown on Islamic fundamentalist groups such as Hamas and extradite "wanted murderers" to Israel.
An anonymous telephone caller told police Hamas carried out the Tel Aviv suicide bombing.

Israel army radio said the bomber was a 28-year-old Palestinian from the Israeli-controlled West Bank village of Sourif. Israel clamped a curfew on Sourif and also imposed a closure on the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
The attack came amid heightened Israeli-Palestinian tension over the groundbreaking on Tuesday of a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
"We will continue to fight violence and will continue to preserve security and stability," Dahlan, Palestinian Preventive Security chief in Gaza, said earlier on Friday.
"But Israel has to understand that for security measures to succeed there must be peace and the right environment has to prevail."
Arafat will leave on a scheduled trip to Pakistan on Saturday despite recent events, a senior PLO official said.
Palestinians have accused Netanyahu of fomenting unrest by forging ahead with the Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
A Hamas leader freed by the Palestinian Authority last week in Gaza told a rally after the attack that only bombs could stop Israel's settlement drive.

Ibrahim al-Makadmeh, whom Arafat released from jail this week to Israeli protests, was imprisoned as part of a crackdown on Hamas and Islamic Jihad after a wave of suicide attacks that killed 59 people in Israel last year.
In Helsinki, U.S. President Bill Clinton, after a summit with Russian President Boris Yeltsin, condemned the attack and said violence had no place in the Middle East peace process.
"I condemn it...," Clinton told a news conference. "There is no place for such acts of terror and violence in the peace process."

The U.S. embassy in Tel Aviv and consulate general in Jerusalem "strongly advised" Americans in Israel to be wary of possible attacks. A statement said U.S. citizen in Israel should avoid large crowds and political demonstrations.
